cards.title: Replace Demographic Profiles With Situational Avatars
cards.summary: Why broad demographic targeting fails and how to build avatars around trigger moments, failed solutions, and identity loss instead.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why creatives or offers aren't differentiating, or when starting avatar research from scratch.
steps: Recognize the failure mode: a demographic like '30+ year old women with knee pain' is not an avatar. The source's test is that a million other products and creatives target the same label, so nothing about yours stands out and there's no leverage against billion-dollar competitors.

Test any avatar you have by asking: what do they vent to a friend about? What products have they already tried? What promises are they sick of hearing? If you can't answer, you don't understand the customer, which is why ad concepts feel like brainstorming instead of problem-solving.
Build the avatar around a specific scenario, e.g. a knee-surgery patient whose physical therapy didn't work and who now wants a holistic solution fitting her daily life.

Anchor the avatar in four layers: the pain, the failed attempts, what they actually want, and day-to-day struggles, including restricted identity activities (e.g. can no longer ice skate with friends).
Note the source's claim: if you don't have a genuinely superior product, niching down on the avatar is the only remaining way to win; the strongest case is to have both.
The source's stated end goal: make the target feel the offer is 'one of one and bespoke to them' even when the underlying product is generic.
caveats: The source treats this as a universal baseline (every avatar needs quoted evidence, a trigger moment, and a job statement), but only claims broad avatars hurt you when you lack a superior product, not as an absolute law.
The number of avatars is not universal; how many you need depends on your business.

cards.title: Mine Competitor 1-Star Reviews for Failure and Trust Markers
cards.summary: Extracting explicit mechanical flaws, trust breaks, and repeated claims from 1-star competitor reviews to feed ad hooks and objections.
cards.use_when: Sourcing granular complaints, objections, and physical product friction before writing creatives or landing pages.
steps: Search Amazon (and wherever else your category is reviewed) for 1-star reviews on competitor listings.

Catalog explicit failure points and mechanical friction verbatim, e.g. 'I was in serious pain and couldn't get the brace off my knee fast enough' — the source treats this kind of complaint as ad-ready material.
Log broken trust markers: things customers say they no longer believe, and repeated product claims that have become exhausted through overuse.
Log recurring venting topics and objections; the source argues these are typically skipped and then reinvented from scratch by marketers.
Look for language patterns that reveal an angle most competitors aren't targeting, e.g. reviews mentioning post-knee-surgery use as an underexploited hook.
Feed the collected phrases into the pre-lander, landing page, and creative so the messaging mirrors what buyers already said rather than what you brainstormed.
caveats: Reviews reveal prior-product failures and objections, not necessarily your own product's performance; don't present competitor flaws as proven claims about you.
The source gives one illustration ('couldn't get the brace off fast enough'), not a guaranteed winning hook — treat it as evidence of a pattern to verify in your own category.

cards.title: Run Direct Phone Calls and Post-Purchase Surveys at Scale
cards.summary: The source's core sourcing routine: continuous outbound contact with existing buyers plus an automated Shopify survey to surface unvarnished lifestyle limitations.
cards.use_when: When you have buyers and need primary evidence of day-to-day friction, concerns, and language you can't get from reviews alone.
steps: Set up a post-purchase survey on Shopify that fires after someone buys (the source also mentions email follow-up).
Do continuous phone outreach to existing buyers rather than a one-off study; the source cites a nine-figure friend whose whole team still calls customers just to ask how everything is going.
DM buyers and ask directly what their concerns are; the source calls this underrated and specifically notes to ask what surprises them.
Ask about day-to-day lifestyle limitations, such as being unable to participate in a defining hobby or sport, not just symptoms.
Watch for patterns across responses: recurring frustrations, specific phrases, broken trust markers, and product claims people no longer believe.
Treat call and survey output as the substrate for messaging across creatives, offer, and landing page — the source's framing is that this intel is the alternative to running on assumptions.
caveats: The nine-figure team call routine is an example of a practice at scale, not a guaranteed conversion result.
Phone and DM research requires buyer volume and staff time; the source ties the payoff to how deep you're willing to go relative to competitors using generic phrasing.

cards.title: Mine Condition-Specific Reddit Forums and Niche Groups
cards.summary: Using community forums as a source of clinical vocabulary, condition-specific pain points, and untapped angles.
cards.use_when: Researching a health, hobby, or subculture niche where customers congregate and describe their situation in their own terms.
steps: Identify condition-specific or problem-specific forums (Reddit is the example given) rather than generic social feeds.
Read what people actually discuss, e.g. 'post-op knees hurt', and log the phrasing as candidate creative copy.
Segment further by which condition or which life consequence to target: inability to do the job versus inability to play sports are described as very different avatars.

Harvest specialized procedural vocabulary, e.g. 'patellar tendon graft'. The source's claim is that a person who has that exact procedure will feel instantly seen by the term, while a general audience won't.
Use forum-level specificity to test narrow angles, e.g. post-knee-surgery recovery for knee braces.
Layer forum research with other sources (Amazon reviews, Google searches, social platforms) rather than relying on one community.
caveats: The source advises researching as many places as possible, not just one; a single forum risks an unrepresentative slice.
Specialized terms only work when your target actually uses them — verify the term's prevalence in the community before building a hook on it.

cards.title: Match Phrasing to the Age Cohort and Platform
cards.summary: Same condition, different cohort, different words: catalog exact vernacular differences so ads sound like the customer, not the marketer.
cards.use_when: Writing ad copy and choosing channels for a specific cohort you're targeting.
steps: Accept that a 20-year-old and a 50-year-old with the same knee problem are different avatars with different day-to-day scenarios and different phrasing.
For the younger cohort, the motive may be competitive running; for the older cohort, running for fun — map the desire, not just the diagnosis.

Collect the sentences people actually form in the places they spend time: for 50-plus, look at Facebook groups or Amazon; for younger audiences, look at TikTok-specific phrasing. The source warns against using TikTok phrasing for a 50-plus audience.
Record exact phrasing, syntax, and terminology from customer vents rather than inventing copy in a brainstorming session.
Build an avatar record that includes age-cohort language, restricted lifestyle activities, and procedural vocabulary, so anyone writing copy can sound like the buyer.
Cross-check your drafts against the verbatim quotes before shipping.
caveats: The channel mapping (Facebook groups for older, TikTok for younger) is the source's illustrative example, not a validated demographic rule — verify against your own buyer data.
Copying a phrase out of context can misfire; the source's point is congruence with the lived experience, not keyword stuffing.

cards.title: Build Belief Through the Avatar's Sequence of Failed Attempts
cards.summary: Structuring creative and landing-page narratives from the buyer's own journey: problem, past failure, why it failed, then the new mechanism.
cards.use_when: Writing ads or landing pages for a researched avatar and converting objections into hooks.
steps: Open by calling out the avatars precisely, e.g. 'do you have a patellar tendon graft / post-op knee?' — the source calls this the hook that stops the scroll.
Move immediately into scenarios they've lived through, including failed solutions such as physical therapy, and name the failure.
Briefly explain why the previous solution failed (for example, that it doesn't address the core problem), which is where your mechanism becomes credible.
Show, don't just tell: the source insists that what the buyer has failed with (PT, other experts) must be depicted congruently, not just asserted.

Keep creative, pre-lander, and landing page congruent on the same condition and the same journey — the source's example: if the creative targets a patellar tendon issue, the landing page can't switch to arthritis, a totally different condition.

Reuse the same objection-to-hook conversion in everything: a strong pattern is naming the prospect in the hook (the source retells Hormozi-style 'are you a gym owner?' hooks) before delivering the value.
caveats: The source defers hook-writing and script mechanics to a separate topic/module; this card covers the belief sequence, not hook formulas.
Congruence is described as improving conversion, not guaranteeing it; test the sequence rather than assuming a template will scale.

cards.title: Let Avatar Research Make the Offer Feel Bespoke
cards.summary: Reframing: the offer is not just the bundle and price but the expectations and language set through deep avatar understanding.
cards.use_when: Positioning a commodity product against identical competitors, or when testing offers and framing.
steps: Understand that buyers compare against familiarity: if your ad names their exact day-to-day struggle in the moment of need — the source's vivid test is an ad that says 'just got out of the shower?' — it feels like a far better fit than a generic pitch.
Treat the offer as including the framing and expectations, not just the price/promo: the source states the offer is not just '2x2 free one'.
Shift the framed outcome from the condition to the restored identity: instead of 'knee pain', the promise becomes enjoying your youth and running again — a very different desire.
Use the avatar's specific language to position your generic product as one of one and bespoke, so the same product as competitors reads differently.
Run this as a competitive move: competitors use generic phrasing; specificity is the leverage.
Feed avatar research into creative strategy, CRO, offers, and retention — the source argues the gap between your assumed customer and the real one bleeds into everything.
caveats: This is the source's positioning opinion, not a universal law: it explicitly notes a genuinely superior product also wins, so you don't have to rely on avatar niche alone.
Framing cannot rescue a product that fails the stated job; the approach is about congruence and specificity, not manufactured claims.

cards.title: Set the Universal Avatar Baseline: Quotes, Trigger, Job
cards.summary: A minimum evidence standard for every avatar record so personas don't drift back into demographic fields with no job.
cards.use_when: Creating or auditing avatar documents, and onboarding writers or media buyers to them.
steps: Require quoted evidence for each avatar: verbatim language drawn from reviews, forums, surveys, calls, or DMs.
Require a trigger moment: the situation in which the person enters the market (the source's example is post-knee-surgery, when PT failed).
Require a job statement: what progress the person is trying to make in their day-to-day life, including restored identity markers such as a sport or hobby.
Reject persona templates that contain only demographics and no job, and reject broad segmentation without situational context or failed past attempts.
Follow the source's stated baseline: quoted evidence, a trigger moment, and a job statement for every avatar — this part is universal, while the number of avatars is not.
Keep the record usable by writers: store the phrasing, the restricted activities, and the specific terminology so copy can be built directly from it.
caveats: The source presents this baseline as its own standard, not a measured benchmark; treat it as a discipline for research quality.
Avatar-count guidance is explicitly not universal in the source — don't force one uniform number across markets.
